title: Types of skin lesions — Blisters and pustules
content:
Types of skin lesions — Blisters and pustules

Blisters and pustules are both fluid-filled bumps on the skin, but they contain different types of
fluid.
Blister (vesicle or bulla): A raised lesion filled with clear or yellowish fluid. Small
blisters are referred to as vesicles, while larger ones are called bullae. Blisters may
result from friction, burns, infections, or various skin diseases. They are often fragile and
may rupture easily, leading to open sores or crusting.
Pustule: A small bump on the skin that contains pus.
subtopic: Chapter 1: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Types of skin lesions — Other important skin signs
content:
Types of skin lesions — Other important skin signs

In addition to the six key types of skin lesions described above, there are other skin changes
that may support the identification or description of specific conditions.
Erythema: This is redness of the skin resulting from increased blood flow to the affected
area. It may indicate irritation, infection, inflammation, or an allergic reaction. The
affected skin may feel warm, tender, or painful to the touch.
Scales: Dry flakes or peeling of the outer layer of the skin (stratum corneum). They are
often observed on patches or plaques and may indicate chronic inflammation, skin
irritation, or the healing phase of a skin condition.
Hyperkeratosis: Thickening and hardening of the outer layer of the skin (epidermis) due
to excessive production of keratin. The affected area may feel rough, hard, or raised,
and is commonly associated with long-standing or chronic skin conditions.
Changes in skin pigmentation: Alterations in skin colour may occur as part of a skin
disease or during the healing process. These changes can vary in degree and
distribution:
Hyperpigmentation: Darkening of the skin or areas with increased skin colour.
Hypopigmentation: Lightening of the skin or areas with reduced skin colour,
appearing pale.
Depigmentation: Complete loss of skin colour, resulting in white patches.
subtopic: Chapter 1: Basics of seeing a patient with skin lesions
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Algorithms - using key skin signs for screening and diagnosis
content:
Algorithms - using key skin signs for screening and diagnosis

This section provides algorithms to support the screening and diagnosis of patients presenting
with skin lesions. The algorithms are organized according to six key types of skin lesions as
starting points: lumps, ulcers, swelling, patches, plaques, and blisters.
Each algorithm guides you through potential causes to help narrow down the diagnosis and
determine appropriate management.
These tools are designed to support clinical decision-making, helping you recognize conditions,
identify next steps, and determine when referral is necessary:
Green indicates treatment can be initiated at your level.
Yellow indicates referral is recommended.
Red indicates urgent referral is needed.
Be aware of the limitation of the algorithms:
The algorithms do not cover all diseases. If you see a condition that is not included or
are uncertain about the diagnosis, refer the patient for further evaluation.
Symptoms can fluctuate over time and may not always be consistent.
The algorithms are based on the typical presentation of each skin disease. However, some
conditions may present atypically and not match the features described here. This is particularly
common in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with HIV/AIDS, diabetes,
or older age, who may show less typical signs. Atypical presentations are an important
indication for referral and further clinical assessment.
When you should refer a patient to a hospital or to a specialist:
When you see signs and symptoms of acute infection or inflammation;
When you find your patient to be severely ill;
When your patient has symptoms other than those on the skin; for example, high fever,
joint pain, etc.;
When the skin condition looks atypical;
When you cannot make a diagnosis; and
When your patient is not responding to treatment and not improving.
Screening & Diagnostic Decision Pathways
Note: The algorithm pathways show typical characteristics of each disease. Not all signs &
symptoms will be present in every patient, and presentations may vary.
This chapter describes the major skin NTDs in the South-East Asia Region. Signs and
symptoms of each disease are provided in alignment with the questions introduced in Chapter
1.
Emphasizing a skin sign and symptom-based approach, wherein the diagnosis is derived from
an analysis of symptoms, this chapter underlines the importance of understanding the signs
presented by patients affected by skin NTDs. By adopting this method, you can effectively
navigate the diagnostic process - prioritizing the recognition of signs and symptoms, considering
potential diagnoses and subsequently taking the next steps to confirm the diagnosis, including
making referrals. To enhance the learning experience, case examples are available in
ANNEXURE 2, serving as valuable resources for training sessions.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — What is leprosy?
content:
Leprosy — What is leprosy?

Leprosy, also known as Hansen's disease, is a chronic skin infection caused by the bacteria
called Mycobacterium (M.) leprae. The disease mainly affects the skin and the peripheral
nerves. In some cases, it can also affect multiple organs including the eyes and the upper
respiratory tract. Leprosy can occur in people of any age, ranging from early infancy to very old
age. The disease is curable and treatment in the early stages can prevent disability.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — How is it transmitted?
content:
Leprosy — How is it transmitted?

Leprosy is likely transmitted via droplets from the nose and mouth during close and frequent
contact with untreated cases. Even when infected, most individuals do not develop the disease
as their immunity can fight the bacteria. Only those who have low or abnormal immunity against
the bacteria develop the disease.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Leprosy — What are the common symptoms?

The symptoms of leprosy include those that appear on the skin and in the peripheral nerves.
The incubation period (time between initial exposure to the infectious agent and development of
symptoms) of leprosy can range from a few years to, sometimes, more than several decades.
How a patient manifests the disease largely depends on his/her immune response against the
bacteria and this leads to a wide variety of its symptoms. Initial symptoms may go unnoticed by
patients - this is common as there can be subtle changes to the skin or because they are
asymptomatic. The symptoms progress very slowly. Patients may first come to care because of
leprosy reactions (see section 2.1.5.).
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — Symptoms of the skin
content:
Leprosy — Symptoms of the skin

Leprosy can affect the skin in many different ways. Common signs include pale
(hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch(es), as well as multiple lumps on the face and body.
These skin lesions may have a dry or scaly surface. Importantly, loss of sensation or tingling
sensation over the extremities is a sign of peripheral neuropathy and should raise suspicion for
leprosy.
Onset: Chronic, progresses very slowly.
Skin lesions: Can include any type of skin lesions.
Distribution:
Localization - varies and may be localized or widely distributed.
Site - can occur on any part of the body.
Symmetry - often asymmetric in PB-type leprosy, and symmetric in MB-type
leprosy (see section 2.1.4).
Texture:
Surface - often dry and/or scaly; may show loss of hair over the skin patch and
plaques.
Border - may be well-defined or ill-defined (When a skin lesion has a
“well-defined” border, it means that you can clearly see where the lesion ends
and the normal skin begins. When the border is “ill-defined”, it is harder to tell
where the lesion stops and the normal skin starts because the boundary between
the two is blurry).
Sensation: Numbness, loss or reduced sensation to the touch, pain and temperature
(cold or hot) over skin lesions; tingling sensation over the extremities.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — Symptoms related to the peripheral nerve damage
content:
Leprosy — Symptoms related to the peripheral nerve damage

There are not many skin diseases that present with peripheral nerve damage or enlargement,
so if you find any symptoms suggestive of nerve damage or enlargement with a skin lesion, the
diagnosis of leprosy becomes more likely. Peripheral nerve damage in leprosy is the cause of
disabilities and deformities - the long-term consequences of the disease and therefore, it is
important to assess the presence of peripheral nerve damage not just for diagnosis but also for
long-term follow-up on the disease.
The symptoms of peripheral nerve damage include:
numbness or tingling of hands and feet;
dryness of the eyes or difficulty in closing the eyelids;
weakness in the muscles;
reduced sensation to the touch, pain and temperature (cold or hot);
enlargement of the nerves;
painful or tender nerves ("neuritis").
Under normal conditions, peripheral nerves are neither visible nor palpable. However, in leprosy,
affected nerves may become enlarged and can sometimes be seen or felt during physical
examination. Conducting a thorough and careful sensory assessment is essential, as many
patients in the early stages of leprosy may be unaware of their sensory loss.
Body parts to check for nerve enlargement: Supraorbital, Supratrochlear, Cervical, Median,
Ulnar, Sural, Posterior tibial, Great auricular, Supraclavicular, Radial, Radial cutaneous,
Common peroneal.
Patients with leprosy can easily develop wounds or burns on the hands or feet because they
cannot feel pain or temperature.
Different signs of leprosy: Pale patch, Multiple patches, Plaque, Lumps on the skin, Ear
thickening, Lagophthalmos (inability to properly close the eyelids due to the weakness),
Painless ulcer, Finger weakness, Wrist/foot drop.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Leprosy — How is it diagnosed?

A case of leprosy is diagnosed when an individual has at least one of the three cardinal signs:
1.​ Skin lesion(s) with definite loss or decreased sensation
2.​ Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness in the
muscles supplied by that nerve; and
3.​ Microscopic detection of acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear (SSS).
How to check for sensory loss in leprosy?
Loss of sensation is one of the earliest and most important signs of leprosy. A simple test can be
carried out using a wisp of cotton or the rounded end of a ballpoint pen. With the patient's eyes
closed, gently touch the skin on and around any suspected patch, and ask the patient to
indicate when they feel the touch. Always compare the sensation over the suspected patch with
areas of normal skin. If sensation is reduced or absent on the patch, the patient should be
referred for further evaluation.
Classification of leprosy
Leprosy can be classified into two types: paucibacillary and multibacillary. The differences in
symptoms exist due to originating from the differences in patients' immune response against M.
leprae.
Paucibacillary (PB) type: defined as a case of leprosy with 1-5 skin lesions.
Multibacillary (MB) type: defined as a case of leprosy with six or more skin lesions or
with nerve involvement (pure neuritis or any number of skin lesions and neuritis) or with
the demonstrated presence of bacilli in a slit-skin smear.
The treatment duration varies between the two types and therefore, it is important to
differentiate the two. Slit-skin smears are positive only in the MB type, when there are many
bacteria in the skin lesions.
What is a slit-skin smear?
It is a method to confirm diagnosis of leprosy, which involves taking samples of body exudates
from 6 routine sites (both earlobes, elbows, and knees), as well as from typical lesions (skin
patches, nodules, etc.) from a suspected patient. These samples are then examined under a
microscope to check for the presence of M. leprae, which looks like slender red rods either
singly or in bundles. The Ziehl-Neelsen stain is also used for diagnosis of tuberculosis, and the
same skills and resources can be applied in diagnosing leprosy.
Differential Diagnoses
Pauci-bacillary (PB) leprosy: Vitiligo, Tinea versicolor, Pityriasis alba, Post inflammatory
hypopigmentation, Lichen planus, Psoriasis vulgaris, Discoid lupus erythematosus.
Multi-bacillary (MB) leprosy: Syphilis, PKDL, Mycosis fungoides, Erythema nodosum,
Erythema multiforme, Neurofibromatosis (von Recklinghausen's disease), Psoriasis
vulgaris, Secondary syphilis.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — What is a leprosy reaction?
content:
Leprosy — What is a leprosy reaction?

Leprosy reactions are inflammatory conditions occurring in the disease due to immune response
against M. leprae, the causative bacteria. In general, immune response is a defense mechanism
of the human body to attack and destroy the germ, but, in some situations, such as in leprosy
reaction, it can overreact or mistakenly attack the human body parts causing inflammatory
symptoms.
There are two types of leprosy reactions – type 1 reaction or reversal reaction and type 2
reaction or erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL). In type 1 reaction, the pre-existing lesions may
worsen and show up as oedema and/or erythema. In type 2 reaction, patients abruptly develop
new lesions, usually very painful erythematous nodules underneath the skin. They may also
present with systemic symptoms, including high fever, joint pains, swelling of lymph nodes and
inflammation of the eyes. In both reaction types, neuritis may occur, which may lead to lifelong
nerve damage. Both reactions need immediate referral to a specialized centre for management.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — How can leprosy be treated?
content:
Leprosy — How can leprosy be treated?

Treat with multidrug therapy (MDT) monthly blister pack that consists of three drugs - rifampicin,
dapsone and clofazimine, for the duration of:
6 months for a paucibacillary case (1-5 skin lesions); and
12 months or more for a multibacillary case (six or more skin lesions or any nerve
involvement).
(In countries updating their leprosy treatment guidelines [WHO, 2018], two MDT options are
available: PB regimen [rifampicin and dapsone] and MB regimen [rifampicin, dapsone and
clofazimine]).
In case of leprosy reaction (suspected/proven): Refer the patient immediately to a
specialist. The patient may need treatment with oral corticosteroids or other
anti-inflammatory medication.
Self-care and rehabilitation: Tell the patient about the importance of self care for affected
eyes, hands and feet, and keeping them in good condition.
Wear soft shoes or sandals that have thick outer soles and comfortable insoles.
In the morning and evening every day, examine hands and feet carefully for any
wounds and early signs of muscle weakness.
Soak hands and feet in lukewarm (not hot) water for 10-20 minutes. After
soaking, rub some oil on the skin of hands and feet for example, petroleum jelly
or vegetable oils, such as palm oil, groundnut oil, coconut oil and sunflower oil.
Protect the eyes against dust, sunlight and dryness. During the day, wear
glasses, a hat or a scarf. At night, sleep under a net or a blanket and tie a cloth
loosely over the eyes, if they do not close properly (lagophthalmos).
In case of wounds: Check Chapter 4 on "Managing wounds" (page 95) and advise
self-care for the prevention or worsening of impairments.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leprosy — How can leprosy be prevented from spreading?
content:
Leprosy — How can leprosy be prevented from spreading?

Leprosy is one of the least infectious diseases, with a very low risk of transmission. The most
effective way to prevent the spread of leprosy is through early detection and prompt treatment of
infectious cases, particularly those with multibacillary leprosy, who are known to transmit the
disease. Multidrug therapy (MDT) not only cures leprosy but also interrupts its transmission.
Contact tracing is an important preventive strategy, especially in high-endemic areas, to help
reduce the number of new cases in the community. WHO currently recommends that eligible
individuals who are in close contact with a confirmed leprosy case may receive preventive
treatment, such as single dose rifampicin, to lower their risk of developing the disease.
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of leprosy:
Support initiating the treatment of the patient and monitor until he/she completes the
treatment course.
Fill in and submit the reporting form.
Look for any signs of reactions and any new onset of nerve function impairment.
Watch closely for any drug-induced adverse effects, including hypersensitivity reaction
(Dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome: Potentially life-threatening adverse reaction to
dapsone, characterized by fever, skin rash, and internal organ involvement. Clinical
features may include jaundice, widespread skin eruption or exfoliation, lymph node
enlargement, and anaemia. This reaction typically occurs within a few weeks to up to six
months after starting MDT. Immediate referral to a higher-level health facility is
essential). Look for signs such as skin redness and peeling, fever and jaundice. Refer to
a higher centre, if you see any of these signs.
If consent is obtained from the diagnosed individual, go to the patient's home and screen
for any other cases in close contact.
Refer the patient to a specialist, if leprosy reaction is suspected.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on implementation of further strategies.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What is leishmaniasis?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What is leishmaniasis?

Leishmaniasis is a parasitic skin infection caused by a group of protozoan parasites known as
Leishmania. It is transmitted by female sandflies. About 20 species of Leishmania are known to
cause disease in humans.
Leishmaniasis is broadly classified into three main types, based on the part of the body
affected:
1.​ Cutaneous leishmaniasis: affects the skin and causes lumps, plaques, or ulcers.
2.​ Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis: affects the skin and mucous membranes, such as the
mouth and nose.
3.​ Visceral leishmaniasis: affects internal organs, such as the liver, spleen, and bone
marrow, and can be life-threatening if not treated.
Post kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a skin condition that can occur after treatment for
visceral leishmaniasis. It appears as skin lesions and may play a role in ongoing transmission of
the disease.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it transmitted?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it transmitted?

Leishmaniasis is transmitted through the bite of female sandflies. These sandflies become
infected with protozoan parasites while feeding on the blood of an infected individual and then
transmit the parasites to a new host (humans) during subsequent blood meals.
How do sandflies look like? Sandflies are tiny insects around 1.5-3 mm in size. It is smaller than
regular mosquitoes and can be difficult to see by the naked eye. They actively feed on blood at
dawn and dusk. Sandflies live in animal burrows, caves, and in peri-domestic settings like in
wall cracks.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What are the common symptoms?

Clinical features of cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) can vary depending on the region and species
involved. The disease usually begins as a red papule at the site of the sandfly bite, as a single
lesion, although multiple lesions can occur. Over the course of weeks to months, the papule
progresses to a painless crusted nodule, plaque or ulcer, often with raised edges forming a
"volcano-like" appearance.
Onset: Usually 2-4 weeks following the bite
Skin lesions: Red papule at the site of sandfly bite; progress to plaque/ulceration with
crusted surface "volcano-like"
Distribution: Often on the exposed sites
Texture: Early lesion smooth; late lesion rough
Sensation: Asymptomatic or mildly painful, if ulcerated
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it diagnosed?

Diagnosis of CL is based on clinical signs and, when possible, laboratory tests. Clinically,
suspicion of CL arises from factors such as residing in high-endemic regions, recent trips to
areas where the disease is common and potential exposure to sandfly bites in the weeks or
months preceding symptoms.
To confirm the diagnosis, skin samples can be taken using slit smear or biopsy. These are
examined under a microscope to look for the Leishmania parasite. In some settings, special
cultures or PCR testing may also be used to confirm the diagnosis and identify the species.
Differential diagnoses of cutaneous leishmaniasis: Leprosy, Cutaneous tuberculosis,
Sarcoidosis, Lupus erythematosus, Skin cancer.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How can cutaneous leishmaniasis be treated?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How can cutaneous leishmaniasis be treated?

In many cases, cutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) can heal on its own, but it may leave permanent
scars, especially on the face or other visible areas.
*Presence of one or more of these features may classify a case as Complex CL.
Simple CL (mild cases): A “wait and watch” approach, providing only wound care
without specific treatment, may be enough.
Keep the lesion clean and dry.
Teach the patient how to provide simple wound care (see Chapter 4).
Ask the patient to return for regular follow-up.
Complex CL: Refer the patient to a hospital or specialist for further treatment.
Local treatment options (referral centers): Cryotherapy (freezing), Heat therapy,
Topical or intralesional medications.
Systemic treatments: Oral miltefosine, Antimonial injections, Amphotericin B, Oral
azoles (limited effectiveness).
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — What are the common symptoms?

Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a skin condition that can occur months to years
after treatment for visceral leishmaniasis (VL), most commonly within 1-2 years.
It presents with multiple hypopigmented patches or lumps. These lesions may appear alone or
in combination, and are usually painless. In rare cases, nodules may ulcerate and leave scars.
Distribution of the lesions are usually symmetrical and can affect the face, the extremities, the
trunk, the genitalia and even the tongue. On the face, the lesions are distributed mostly around
the mouth or the nose. Some patients may develop photosensitivity, where skin becomes red
with sun exposure.
Onset: Few months to years after VL is cured
Skin lesions: Multiple hypopigmented patches; sun-exposed areas (e.g., face)
Distribution: Usually symmetrical
Texture: Patches: texture same as that of normal skin; Lumps: swollen and glossy
(juicy)
Sensation: Asymptomatic (unlike leprosy)
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How is it diagnosed?

The diagnosis of PKDL is based on the clinical signs and, when available, laboratory tests.
PKDL should be suspected in patients with:
Skin lesions (hypopigmented patches, papules, or nodules) in a symmetrical pattern;
A history of VL or residence in a VL-endemic area; and
No sensory loss or nerve thickening, which helps distinguish it from leprosy.
Slit-skin smear or skin biopsy can be used to look for the parasite under the microscope. If
available, PCR testing can help confirm the diagnosis. The rK39 rapid diagnostic test (RDT) can
help support a diagnosis of PKDL by showing past VL infection. However, since it may stay
positive even after treatment, it cannot confirm PKDL or rule out other causes like leprosy.
Differential Diagnosis of PKDL
Erythematous papule/plaque and nodule: Leprosy / Hansen's disease, Sarcoidosis,
Secondary syphilis, Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, Cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia.
Hypopigmented macules and patches: Pityriasis versicolor, Leprosy / Hansen's disease,
Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation following Guttate psoriasis, Pityriasis rosea,
Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica.
Photosensitivity: Systemic lupus erythematosus, Rosacea.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How can leishmaniasis be prevented from spreading?
content:
Leishmaniasis, including cutaneous leishmaniasis and post kala-azar dermal — How can leishmaniasis be prevented from spreading?

There are two important pillars for preventing the spread of leishmaniasis: control of the human
reservoir and vector control.
Control of reservoir: The central pillar of PKDL control rests on early case detection
through active case detection, and complete treatment of patients affected by VL and
PKDL. It is critically important that VL patients are monitored at least three years after
treatment for possible development of PKDL.
Vector control: Control of sandflies in domestic and peridomestic transmission habitats
through deployment of chemicals (i.e. indoor residual sprays and long lasting insecticidal
nets), environmental management including local sanitation and improved housing, and
personal protection (i.e. bed nets and clothing that covers the skin) are the methods of
preventing the spread.
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of cutaneous
leishmaniasis:
Support initiating treatment of the patient and monitor until treatment is completed.
Fill in and submit the reporting form.
For PKDL: If the patient consents, screen other household members, and then, if
appropriate, conduct a house-to-house search in the immediate neighbourhood.
Refer the patient to specialists if the lesion is not improving or shows signs of complex
CL.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on implementation of further strategies.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — What is lymphatic filariasis?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — What is lymphatic filariasis?

Lymphatic filariasis (LF), commonly known as elephantiasis, is caused by infection by parasitic
worms known as nematodes (roundworms), including Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and
Brugia timori.
These parasites target the lymphatic system, an essential component of the body’s fluid
regulation and immune function. When the lymphatic system is damaged, fluid can accumulate
in various parts of the body, most commonly the legs, arms, breasts, or genitalia—leading to
chronic swelling and disfigurement. Lymphatic filariasis is one of the leading causes of
permanent disability globally and has significant social and economic consequences for affected
individuals and communities.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — How is it transmitted?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — How is it transmitted?

Lymphatic filariasis is spread from person to person by mosquitoes. Adult worms live in the
human lymph nodes or vessels, where they mate and produce millions of baby worms, known
as microfilariae. These microfilariae circulate in the person’s blood and are taken up by a
mosquito when it bites an infected individual. Inside the mosquito, the microfilariae grow and
develop into infective worms. When the mosquito bites another person, these infective worms
are passed on from the mosquito to the new person. The worms live for about 5–7 years or
sometimes longer. Prolonged exposure to multiple mosquito bites, spanning several months to
years, is needed for lymphatic filariasis to develop.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — What are the common symptoms?

Lymphatic filariasis often causes no symptoms in the early stages. Damage to the lymph
vessels happens over time. When clinical symptoms do appear, they typically develop years
after the initial infection.
Patients with lymphoedema are at risk of secondary bacterial infections. Breaks in the skin may
allow the entry of bacteria into the body. This can be from eczema, fungal infections between
the toes, ulcers or even small injuries. These are called bacterial entry lesions and can cause
recurrent infections, also known as “acute attacks” or “red legs”. Repeated attacks can lead to
thickening of the skin and hardening of the limb, with secondary skin changes such as nodules
and warty growths. This can progress to a condition known as elephantiasis, where the affected
limb becomes enlarged and deformed.
The most common clinical manifestations include:
Lymphoedema: Swelling of body parts due to fluid accumulation, most commonly
affecting the legs, but also observed in the arms, breasts, or genitalia. The affected area
may feel heavy, tight, or uncomfortable.
Hydrocele: Swelling of the scrotum in men, caused by fluid buildup around the testes.
Swelling of the breasts or vulva: This can occur in women, although it is less common.
Onset: Chronic, progresses very slowly, besides acute attacks
Skin lesions: Swelling of the legs, arms, (rarely) breasts or genitalia; nodules; skin folds
in legs and arms; “mossy foot”
Distribution: Usually unilateral; if affected on both sides, then usually asymmetrical
Texture: Non-pitting oedema; darkening of the skin; thickening of the skin; warty
overgrowth
Sensation: Heaviness of the limb; painful during acute attack
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — How is it diagnosed?

The standard method for diagnosing active infection of lymphatic filariasis is the detection of
microfilariae (larval stage of the parasite) by microscopic examination of thick blood smears
($20\text{--}60\text{ }\mu\text{L}$) obtained from a finger-prick sample. In most endemic areas
of Asia, microfilariae circulate in the peripheral blood with a nocturnal periodicity (they are
present in higher numbers at night), so blood collection should be done between 10:00 p.m. and
2:00 a.m. to maximize diagnostic accuracy. However, in areas where subperiodic W. bancrofti or
Brugia species are endemic such as parts of Thailand and Indonesia, microfilariae may be
detectable during daytime hours as well, and timing of blood collection should be adjusted
accordingly.
WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are available to detect circulating filarial
antigens specific to Wuchereria bancrofti. A positive antigen test indicates an active or recent
infection and is particularly useful in settings where microscopy is not feasible. For Brugia
species, antibody-based card tests are available; however, these tests cannot distinguish
between current and past infections.
As lymphoedema and other chronic manifestations of lymphatic filariasis can develop many
years after the initial infection, laboratory test results may be negative in such cases. In these
instances, diagnosis is made clinically, based on the presence of characteristic signs and
symptoms.
Differential Diagnosis of Lymphatic Filariasis
Extremities:
Primary lymphoedema: present at birth or start after one year or during puberty
or later in adult life
Secondary lymphoedema: cancer, cancer treatment (surgery or radiotherapy),
trauma or fracture, recurring episodes of lymphangitis or cellulitis
Systemic causes of lymphoedema: congestive heart failure, deep venous
thrombosis, kidney diseases, malnutrition, familial and genetic causes
Genitals: Congenital hydrocele, Inguinal hernia
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — How can lymphatic filariasis be treated and managed?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — How can lymphatic filariasis be treated and managed?

Lymphatic filariasis treatment involves two key components: (1) treatment of the underlying
infection, and (2) management of long-term complications through morbidity management and
disability prevention (MMDP).
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — Morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP)
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — Morbidity management and disability prevention (MMDP)

MMDP includes lymphoedema management, treatment of acute attack and surgical
management of hydrocele, alongside treatment for underlying filarial infection. Together, these
interventions form WHO’s Essential Package of Care.
Grading of Lymphoedema (Dreyer Seven-stage classification):
Stage 1: Swelling is reversible overnight (increases during the day, goes away overnight
lying flat).
Stage 2: Swelling is not reversible without lymphoedema management.
Stage 3: Shallow skin folds (base of fold can be seen when leg/foot moves).
Stage 4: Knobs (presence of bumps, lumps, or protrusions of skin).
Stage 5: Deep skin folds (base of fold cannot be seen when leg/foot moves).
Stage 6: Mossy lesions (small elongated or rounded growths clustered together).
Stage 7: Unable to care for self or perform daily routine activities independently.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — Lymphoedema management
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — Lymphoedema management

Hygiene: Wash the affected areas at least once daily with soap and clean water at room
temperature, and dry carefully with a clean towel or gauze. Wash/dry carefully between
toes, folds, and nodules.
Skin and wound care: Look for entry lesions (injuries, wounds, fungal infections
between toes or under folds). Apply topical medications (antiseptics, antibiotic creams,
or antifungal creams).
Elevation: Raise the affected area at night and during the day when possible to promote
lymphatic flow.
Exercise: Exercise the affected area regularly with low-intensity movement of the joints.
Wear comfortable footwear: Protect feet from injury; avoid tight shoes that cause
abrasions.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — Treatment of acute attacks
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — Treatment of acute attacks

Educate the patient about seeking immediate care when the affected limbs get red, swollen
and/or painful (acute attack). These are signs of secondary infection needing immediate
treatment with antibiotics. Refer them immediately to a health facility.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — Management of hydrocele
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — Management of hydrocele

Hydrocele is managed through surgical intervention (hydrocelectomy). Refer patients to a
specialist or hospital equipped for safe surgical care.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Lymphatic filariasis — How can lymphatic filariasis be prevented from spreading?
content:
Lymphatic filariasis — How can lymphatic filariasis be prevented from spreading?

In endemic areas, mass drug administration (MDA) is conducted once a year for the entire
at-risk population to reduce microfilariae in the blood and interrupt transmission by mosquitoes.
In addition, avoid mosquito bites.
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of lymphatic
filariasis:
Assess the stage of lymphoedema and confirm the diagnosis with the medical officer.
Initiate self-care for the patients and visit them at their homes, and reinforce whenever
necessary.
Educate the patients and family on self-care.
When acute attacks are suspected, refer the patient to a medical officer/hospital (PHC).
When a hydrocele is diagnosed, educate the patient about surgery and its advantages,
and ensure he/she is referred for surgery by the medical officer to an appropriate health
facility for the procedure.
If a person comes with positive microfilariae or antigen test, make sure that the person
receives the treatment for filarial infection.
Submit the filled-out reporting form.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on delivery of the Essential Package of Care and MMDP activities.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis

Deep mycoses are fungal infections that affect the deeper layers of the skin and, in some cases,
the underlying tissues.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is chromoblastomycosis?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is chromoblastomycosis?

Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic skin infection caused by certain types of fungi that produce
brown pigments (e.g., Phialophora, Fonsecaea, and Cladophialophora species). These fungi
are found in soil, wood and decaying plant materials. It is considered an occupational disease
commonly seen in farmers, forestry workers, and animal handlers.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?

The fungi enter the skin through injuries or wounds (e.g., a puncture with a splinter when
walking barefoot). It does not transmit human-to-human.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?

Usually begins on the foot or leg. Starts as a small, singular, elevated lesion, followed by slow
growth producing crusted, verrucous ("warty") or ulcerated lesions. Satellite lesions may
develop. Itching is usually present. Chronic lesions may lead to squamous cell carcinoma.
Onset: Chronic, very slow
Skin lesions: Papule, nodule, plaque, verrucous or ulcerated lesion
Distribution: Usually single lesion, satellite lesions may be present
Texture: Firm, rough and bumpy surface
Sensation: Frequently very itchy
Types include: Plaque, Cicatricial (Scar-like), Verrucous (Wart-like), Tumorous.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?

Diagnosed by identifying dark brown, thick-walled, round fungal cells under a microscope from
skin scrapings or biopsy. Lesions with small black dots ("cayenne pepper" appearance) are best
for sampling. Fungal culture, PCR, and DNA sequencing may also be used.
Differential diagnosis: Other deep fungal infections (eumycetoma, sporotrichosis), bacterial
infections (tuberculosis, leprosy, syphilis), protozoal infections (CL, PKDL), squamous cell
carcinoma, psoriasis, sarcoidosis, discoid lupus erythematosus.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is mycetoma?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is mycetoma?

Mycetoma is a chronic skin infection caused by fungi (eumycetoma) or bacteria
(actinomycetoma). It occurs in individuals with frequent soil/plant contact.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?

Enters through minor skin injuries like thorn pricks, cuts, or splinters.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?

Begins as firm, painless nodules or a "woody" (hard, thick) swelling beneath the skin. Forms
sinuses draining pus containing "grains". Can destroy muscle and bone if untreated.
Classic triad: Painless, firm subcutaneous swelling; Multiple sinus formations; and Discharge
containing pus and "grains".
Eumycetoma grains: Small, white to black granules.
Actinomycetoma grains: Yellow, orange, or pinkish granules.
Onset: Chronic, very slow
Skin lesions: Nodules, "woody" swelling, sinus, hyperpigmentation
Distribution: Asymmetrical, localized
Texture: Firm, rough and bumpy surface
Sensation: No or moderate pain during early stage, pain during late stage or secondary
infection
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?

Direct microscopic observation of grains from sinus fluid, scrapings, or biopsy. Culture, PCR,
imaging (ultrasound, X-ray, CT, MRI) evaluate bone/tissue depth.
Differential diagnosis: Other deep mycoses, cutaneous TB, osteomyelitis, skin tumors
(squamous cell carcinoma, sarcoma, Kaposi sarcoma).
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is sporotrichosis?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What is sporotrichosis?

A chronic skin infection caused by Sporothrix schenckii, found on rose thorns, hay, moss, twigs,
and soil ("rose gardener's disease").
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it transmitted?

Enters skin via cuts/punctures during contact with contaminated plant material or soil.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — What are the common symptoms?

Starts as a painless red nodule that spreads along lymphatic channels in a "linear" pattern.
Nodules may ulcerate and drain pus.
Onset: Subacute to chronic
Skin lesions: Nodules, nodules with central ulceration, swelling, abscess
Distribution: Asymmetrical, with lesions often spreading in a chain-like pattern
Texture: Firm
Sensation: Little or no pain in early lesions; mild pain may occur with increased severity
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How is it diagnosed?

Suspected by linear lesion distribution. Confirmed by fungal culture or histopathology with
special stains (PAS, Grocott's methenamine silver).
Differential diagnosis: Chromoblastomycosis, mycetoma, CL, nocardiosis, mycobacterial
diseases, cat-scratch disease, leprosy, syphilis, sarcoidosis, pyoderma gangrenosum.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How can deep mycoses be treated?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How can deep mycoses be treated?

Requires long-term treatment. Options include:
Antifungals (itraconazole, terbinafine, voriconazole) or antibiotics for actinomycetoma
Wound care, local heat therapy, cryosurgery, surgical removal of affected tissue, and
rehabilitation.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How can deep mycoses be prevented?
content:
Deep mycoses, including mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and sporotrichosis — How can deep mycoses be prevented?

Wear protective footwear and clothing when working in risk areas.
Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling plants.
Clean and cover skin injuries promptly.
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of deep
mycoses:
Support initiating treatment of the patient and monitor until he/she completes the
treatment course.
Educate the patient and their family on self-care.
Fill in and submit the reporting form.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on implementation of further strategies.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — What is scabies?
content:
Scabies — What is scabies?

Scabies is a skin disease caused by a microscopic mite (Sarcoptes scabiei) about 0.4 mm in
size. Female mites burrow into the skin to lay eggs, leading to allergic reactions that cause
intense itching and skin lesions.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — How is it transmitted?
content:
Scabies — How is it transmitted?

Transmitted primarily through prolonged, direct skin-to-skin contact (household members,
spouses, sexual contact). Indirect transmission via clothing or bedding is uncommon except in
crusted scabies.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Scabies — What are the common symptoms?

Symptoms take up to 6 weeks to appear after initial exposure. Causes intense itching (worse at
night) and a rash. Burrows (thin, thread-like lines) are commonly found in finger webspaces,
palms, and wrists. Scratching can cause secondary impetigo, which may lead to heart/kidney
complications.
Onset: Subacute symptoms (up to 6 weeks post-infestation)
Skin lesions: Papules, nodules, scaling, crusting, erosions, blisters/pustules, and
scabies burrows
Distribution:
Older children/adults: Finger webs, wrists, armpits, nipples, male genitalia,
waist, buttocks (head/neck spared).
Infants/elderly/immunocompromised: May involve head, face, palms, soles.
Texture: Scaly, soft/pus-filled
Sensation: Intensely itchy, worse at night
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Scabies — How is it diagnosed?

Clinical diagnosis based on history of itching at night and contact history. Confirmed by
dermoscopy or skin scrapings showing mites, eggs, or fecal pellets (see IACS criteria in
Annexure 3).
Differential diagnosis: Folliculitis, atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis, drug eruptions,
impetigo, lichen planus, insect bites, lice, urticaria.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — What is crusted scabies?
content:
Scabies — What is crusted scabies?

Also known as Norwegian scabies, a severe, highly contagious form occurring in
immunocompromised individuals (e.g., HIV/AIDS) with thousands to millions of mites. Presents
with thick, scaly, crusted plaques. Itching may be absent or minimal.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — How can scabies be treated?
content:
Scabies — How can scabies be treated?

Treat all family members and close contacts simultaneously.
Option 1 (Oral): Single dose oral ivermectin (do not give to pregnant women or children)
Option 2 (Topical): Benzyl benzoate (adults 25%; children 12.5%) applied for 24 hours,
OR Permethrin 5% cream applied from neck down for 8–12 hours before washing off.
Both treatment options must be repeated 1 week later.
For crusted scabies, combine oral ivermectin and topical treatments with more frequent
dosing.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Scabies — How can scabies be prevented from spreading?
content:
Scabies — How can scabies be prevented from spreading?

Treat all close contacts simultaneously.
Wash bedding and clothing used within 3 days prior to treatment in hot water or iron
them.
Clean mattresses/sofas with a vacuum cleaner and air in the sun.
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of scabies:
Treat the patient with the correct medication.
Fill in and submit the reporting form.
Go to the patient’s home, community and school to screen and identify any other cases.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on implementation of targeted screening and/or mass treatment.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Yaws — What is yaws?
content:
Yaws — What is yaws?

Yaws is a chronic skin infection caused by spiral bacteria Treponema pallidum subspecies
pertenue. It is not sexually transmitted. It mainly affects children under 15 years old (peak: 6–10
years). Affects skin, cartilage, and bones. Curable with a single dose of azithromycin.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Yaws — How is it transmitted?
content:
Yaws — How is it transmitted?

Transmitted by direct skin-to-skin contact with infectious lesions through skin cuts or wounds.
Incubation period is 9–90 days (average 21 days). Facilitated by poor hygiene and crowding.
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Yaws — What are the common symptoms?
content:
Yaws — What are the common symptoms?

Primary yaws: Initial lesion ("mother yaw") appears as an outward-growing warty lump
(papilloma) with a raspberry/cauliflower appearance, which may ulcerate with a red base
and raised edges.
Secondary yaws: Weeks to months later, multiple "daughter yaws" appear. Skin
thickening on palms/soles and bone pain/swelling (dactylitis) can occur.
Tertiary yaws: Occurs years later; can cause severe facial destruction and bone
deformities.
Onset: Subacute
Skin lesions: Papillomas, red-based ulcers, hypopigmented patches, palm/sole skin
thickening
Distribution: Solitary or multiple asymmetric lesions
Texture: Soft, raspberry/cauliflower-like surface
Sensation: Generally painless and non-itchy; palm/sole lesions may cause painful
walking
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Yaws — How is it diagnosed?
content:
Yaws — How is it diagnosed?

Clinical appearance supported by Rapid Diagnostic Tests like the Dual Path Platform (DPP
Syphilis Screen and Confirm Assay) using finger-prick blood. DPP checks treponemal
antibodies (past/present infection) and non-treponemal biomarkers (active infection).
subtopic: Chapter 2: Major skin-related neglected tropical diseases in the South-East Asia Region
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Yaws — How can yaws be prevented from spreading?
content:
Yaws — How can yaws be prevented from spreading?

Total Community Treatment (TCT): Mass distribution of single-dose azithromycin to
endemic communities.
Total Targeted Treatment (TTT): Treating active cases and all close contacts
(household, schoolmates, playmates).
Checklist for front-line health workers: When you have a diagnosed case of yaws:
Treat the patient with the correct medication.
Fill in and submit the reporting form.
Go to the patient’s home, community and school to screen and identify any other cases.
Report to the district/provincial focal point if more patients are identified and seek advice
on implementation of targeted mass treatment.
Region (besides skin NTDs)
This chapter introduces some of the most common skin diseases encountered in communities
across the WHO South-East Asia Region. Conditions are organized by their origin and
pathogenesis, with key clinical features highlighted to help you recognize signs and symptoms.
Because many skin diseases share similar treatment approaches, general management
guidance is provided at the end of each section. Always follow national or regional treatment
protocols when available.
Thinking through differential diagnoses is a critical step in reaching an accurate diagnosis. Even
if a skin lesion looks familiar, always ask yourself: "What else could this be?"
Developing a list of possible diagnoses based on observed signs and symptoms takes both
experience and knowledge. This chapter aims to expand your understanding of a broad range
of skin conditions and sharpen your ability to distinguish between them. Revisit the clinical
images and reflect on what makes one condition different from another.
If a diagnosis is unclear, or if the patient presents with a chronic, treatment-resistant, or
severe condition, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Fungal infections — Common fungal infections – photo gallery with key points
content:
Fungal infections — Common fungal infections – photo gallery with key points

Figure 3.1.1. Pityriasis versicolor
Fungal (yeast) infection
Common in hot, humid climates
Lightly hypopigmented skin patches
Most commonly affects the trunk, neck and/or arms
Sometimes itchy, but can be asymptomatic
Non-infectious
Figure 3.1.2. Tinea corporis ("ringworm")
Fungal (yeast) infection
No worm is involved
A scaly, ring-shaped plaque, typically on the buttocks, trunk, arms and legs
Borders may be slightly raised
Sometimes itchy, but can be asymptomatic
Spreads by direct skin-to-skin contact with an infected person or animal
Figure 3.1.3. Tinea incognito
Fungal (yeast) infection (e.g., tinea corporis) in which the typical appearance of the
lesion is altered due to inappropriate treatment, usually with topical corticosteroids
Compared to classic tinea corporis, lesions in tinea incognito are less scaly, have less
defined or raised edges, and are often more widespread
These atypical features can make diagnosis challenging and require careful
differentiation from other skin conditions
Discontinuing topical corticosteroids is the most important step in management
Figure 3.1.4. Tinea capitis ("ringworm of the scalp")
Fungal (yeast) infection of the scalp and hair
Common in children
Scaly, bald patches on the head, broken hair
Sizes and numbers may vary
Sometimes itchy, but can be asymptomatic
Some cases may result in severe inflammation
Figure 3.1.5. Tinea pedis ("athlete's foot") and tinea unguium ("nail fungus")
Erosions in between toes
Can also present as thick scales covering the sole and/or sides of the feet
Fungal infection of nails presents with deformed nails
Spreads from direct contact with the fungus, for example, using a shared towel or by
walking barefoot in a shared space
Some cases may result in severe inflammation
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Fungal infections — How can fungal infections be treated?
content:
Fungal infections — How can fungal infections be treated?

Fungal skin infections are treated with antifungal medications, which may be applied topically
(as a cream) or taken orally (by mouth). The choice of treatment depends on the type of
infection, its severity, and whether it is widespread or recurrent.
General treatment tips
Keep the skin clean and dry.
Avoid sharing clothes, towels, or personal items.
For mild or localized infections, topical antifungal creams are usually sufficient.
Antifungal medications tend to have a range of side-effects including liver failure. Do not
use these for a prolonged period of time.
Oral antifungal medications may be required for infections that are extensive, persistent,
or involve the scalp or nails.
Continue treatment for at least one week after symptoms have resolved.
Wear loose-fitting clothes.
Note: A detailed list of treatment options is provided in ANNEXURE 4.
Emerging threats: Drug-resistant fungi
The incidence and prevalence of drug-resistant fungi is on the rise! Especially, pathogenic
dermatophytes resistant to terbinafine are widespread not only in the South-East Asian region
where it originated but spreading rapidly throughout the world. Major factors for the
development of anti-fungal resistance is attributed to the widespread and indiscriminate use of
broad-spectrum antifungals in both medicine and agriculture, as well as inadequate adherence
to hygienic practices. There are actions that we can take at an individual level to mitigate this
emergence. It is important that you make efforts to restrict inappropriate anti-fungal
medication usage by limiting unnecessary prescriptions and educating your patients on
their usage. You can also educate your patients and community members in hygienic practices
to cut the infection chain.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Bacterial infections — Common bacterial infections – photo gallery with key points
content:
Bacterial infections — Common bacterial infections – photo gallery with key points

Figure 3.2.1. Impetigo
Very common bacterial skin infection among children
Yellow "honey-coloured" crusts, blisters, often itchy
Affects skin anywhere on the body but most common on the face around the nose and
the mouth
Spreads from direct skin-to-skin contact
Figure 3.2.2. Cellulitis
Bacterial skin infection
Acute onset
Red, swollen limbs, painful
A feeling of warmth in the affected area
Usually unilateral (affects only one side)
Sometimes associated with fever and chills
Infection may spread to inner body and become life threatening
Figure 3.2.3. Abscess
Bacterial skin infection
Painful collection of pus under the skin
Usually single lesion
Sometimes, a pinpoint opening in the centre of the lesion
Sometimes associated with fever and chills
Fluctuant, red, painful and warm to touch
Figure 3.2.4. Skin tuberculosis
Skin infection from M. tuberculosis, the same bacterium that causes pulmonary
tuberculosis (TB)
Long duration
Usually asymptomatic
Limited inflammation (redness, swelling and pain)
Wide variety of skin lesions, including papules, nodules, patches and ulcers
Refer to check for pulmonary TB
Figure 3.2.5. Syphilis
Chronic skin infection caused by spiral bacteria called Treponema pallidum
Commonly spreads through sexual activity
Starts with painless sore in the genital area, anus or mouth
Skin lesions in later stages of the disease include asymptomatic, rough, red rash;
sometimes, there is hair loss
A rosy rash on the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet is characteristic
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Bacterial infections — How can bacterial infections be treated?
content:
Bacterial infections — How can bacterial infections be treated?

Bacterial skin infections are typically managed with antibiotics. The type and route of antibiotics
depend on the specific infection, its severity, and the patient's overall condition. Most mild to
moderate infections respond well to oral antibiotics. Severe cases may require intravenous
antibiotics and referral to a specialist.
General treatment tips
Treat with oral antibiotics for 7–10 days; up to 14 days may be needed in some cases.
If there is poor response or the infection is severe, consider intravenous antibiotics and
refer to a higher-level facility.
Supportive care such as proper wound care, rest, and elevation of the affected area, is
important in all cases.
Note: A detailed list of treatment options is provided in ANNEXURE 4.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Viral infection — Common viral infections – photo gallery with key points
content:
Viral infection — Common viral infections – photo gallery with key points

Varicella (chickenpox)
Figure 3.3.1. & Figure 3.3.2.
Viral infection (Varicella-Zoster virus)
Acute onset, fever from a few days before the skin symptoms
Rash may show in the body and face, and then spread to other parts
May be itchy with blisters all over the body
Mainly in children, if in adults, symptoms can be severe
Highly contagious; an affected individual needs to be isolated until the blisters scab over
with a crust
Can be prevented by vaccine
Herpes zoster (shingles)
Figure 3.3.3. & Figure 3.3.4.
Viral infection (Varicella-Zoster virus)
After chickenpox, the virus hides inside the body and reappears as a single stripe of
blisters when changes to the immune system occur (presence of severe disease, stress,
fatigue, ageing, etc.)
Localized to one side of the body
Very painful; pain may persist for a long time
Usually non-infectious
Figure 3.3.5. Measles (rubeola, morbilli)
Viral infection (measles virus)
Acute onset with fever, often with persistent cough, runny nose, red eyes and sore throat
Rash with small red spots appears 2–3 days after the first fever, spreads from the face
downwards to the arms, the chest and the back, then to the legs
"Koplik spots" inside the mouth
Highly contagious, spreads from person to person by breathing in droplets from an
infected person's coughing or sneezing in air
Isolate an affected individual until five days after the onset of rash
Can be prevented by vaccination
Figure 3.3.6. Mouth herpes (cold sores)
Viral infection (herpes simplex virus type 1)
Grouped, small, fluid-filled blisters on and around the lips
Painful
May recur when changes to the immune system occur (stress, fatigue, hormonal
changes, etc.)
Spreads from person to person by close contact, such as kissing
Genital herpes
Figure 3.3.7. & Figure 3.3.8.
Ulcer on and around the genitalia, usually with well-defined borders
Blisters can also be seen
Enlarged and tender local lymph nodes
Painful
May recur throughout life
Spreads from person to person by close contact, such as sexual contact
Figure 3.3.9. Molluscum contagiosum
Mainly affects children
Small round papules with a dimple in the centre
Smooth and shiny appearance, can come in clusters
Spreads by direct skin-to-skin contact, can spread to another body site by scratching or
shaving
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Viral infection — How can viral infections be treated?
content:
Viral infection — How can viral infections be treated?

Most viral skin infections are self-limiting and resolve without specific medical treatment.
Management usually focuses on relieving symptoms. In some cases, such as herpes simplex or
shingles, antiviral medications can reduce the duration or severity of illness. Vaccination plays a
key role in preventing viral infections such as measles and chickenpox. Promoting vaccine
awareness and uptake is essential for community protection.
General treatment tips
Use antihistamines and fever reducers (e.g., paracetamol) to relieve discomfort.
Avoid giving aspirin to children due to the risk of serious side effects (e.g., Reye's
syndrome).
Antiviral medications may be prescribed for infections such as herpes and shingles.
Advise patients and caregivers to avoid close contact with others while lesions are active
to prevent spread.
Encourage and promote vaccination where available.
Note: A detailed list of treatment options is provided in ANNEXURE 4.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Ectoparasites — Common ectoparasites infections (besides scabies) – photo gallery with key points
content:
Ectoparasites — Common ectoparasites infections (besides scabies) – photo gallery with key points

Figure 3.4.1. Head lice (Pediculosis capitis)
Tiny, wingless insects (lice) that live and feed on the blood from the human scalp; the
female insects lay eggs which stick to hair shafts
Itchiness and irritation of the scalp
Usually in children
Spreads from direct transfer from the hair of a person to the hair of another person
Figure 3.4.2. Pubic lice (Pthirus pubis)
Tiny, wingless insects (lice) that live and feed on the blood attached to the hair in the
pubic area
Sometimes, can be found on coarse hair elsewhere on the body
Itchy
Spreads from person to person, usually through sexual contact
Figure 3.4.3. Bedbugs (Cimex lectularius)
Tiny, wingless insects that live in human domains such as in crevices of floors and walls,
in beddings and in furniture
Feed on human blood mainly at night
Linear or grouped arrangement of papules
Itchy bite reactions often occur on exposed sites
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Ectoparasites — How can ectoparasite infestations be treated?
content:
Ectoparasites — How can ectoparasite infestations be treated?

Ectoparasite infestations can be effectively managed through topical treatments, personal
hygiene, and environmental cleaning. Most cases do not require oral medications. Preventing
reinfestation by treating close contacts and addressing the environment is critical.
General treatment tips
Apply topical treatments (e.g., permethrin, benzyl benzoate) as directed to kill lice or
mites.
Use a fine-toothed comb to remove lice and eggs from the hair.
Wash clothing, bedding, and personal items in hot water and dry at high heat.
Avoid sharing personal items such as combs, hats, towels, or bedding.
For bedbugs, environmental control is essential: pour boiling water on sleeping surfaces,
and wash sheets and blankets on the same day. Avoid using infested items for at least
three weeks.
Note: A detailed list of treatment options is provided in ANNEXURE 4.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Inflammatory disorders — Common inflammatory disorders – photo gallery with key points
content:
Inflammatory disorders — Common inflammatory disorders – photo gallery with key points

Figure 3.5.1. Acne
Inflammation due to blockage of hair follicles and sebaceous glands (comedones)
Common in adolescents and young adults
Occurs due to a combination of factors: endogenous and exogenous hormones, familial
tendency, acne bacteria, etc.
Inflamed papules and pustules on the face, sometimes on the neck, chest and back
Nodules and pseudocysts in severe acne
May leave scars after cure
Figure 3.5.2. (left) and 3.5.3. (right) Eczema/dermatitis
Skin condition that causes patches of itchiness and irritated skin (red, swelling, cracks,
etc.)
Common in all age groups
Sometimes, eczema may occur after contact with a substance, in which case, avoiding
the suspected substance is the most important treatment (contact dermatitis, drug
eruption)
Acute eczema can form fluid-filled blisters
In chronic eczema, the skin may thicken and feel scaly or leathery
Figure 3.5.4. Seborrheic eczema
Common form of eczema that mainly affects the scalp and other areas of the body, such
as the face, sides of the nose, eyebrows, ears, eyelids and chest
