Skin flakes on the scalp and other hairy body parts, red patches covered with flaky
scales
Itchy
Underlying fungal infection with associated inflammation is the main cause
May go without treatment, but in some cases, recurrence is common despite treatment
Figure 3.5.5. Pityriasis alba
Common form of eczema that mainly affects children
Hypopigmented patches with fine flakes
Usually appears on the face, neck, or upper body
Not usually itchy but cosmetic concern
May come and go
Gradually heals on its own before adulthood
Important differential diagnosis of early leprosy
Figure 3.5.6. Prurigo nodularis
Intensely itchy lumps on the skin
Multiple in number
Chronic in nature
Affects skin anywhere in the body
Dome-shaped papules or nodules
Often associated with certain conditions including scabies and atopic dermatitis
Can recur even with treatment
Figure 3.5.7. (left) and 3.5.8. (right) Psoriasis vulgaris
Affects 2%–3% of the total population, the most common type is psoriasis vulgaris
Red, well-defined plaques with silvery white scales
Symmetrically distributed
Affects skin anywhere in the body, but commonly on the knees, elbows, trunk and scalp
Can be associated with joint pains (psoriatic arthritis), nail changes and metabolic
diseases (diabetes, high blood pressure, hyperlipidemia, obesity)
Can be triggered by medications, infection, habits, stress, etc.

source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Inflammatory disorders — How can inflammatory skin conditions be treated?
content:
Inflammatory disorders — How can inflammatory skin conditions be treated?

Inflammatory skin conditions can vary in severity and individual treatment plans – for example,
strength of steroidal ointment (such as hydrocortisone or betamethasone) and duration – should
be discussed with a specialist for chronic conditions.
General treatment tips
Keep the skin moisturized.
Identify and avoid potential triggers such as allergens, irritants, or stress.
Topical corticosteroids (e.g., hydrocortisone or betamethasone) are commonly used to
reduce inflammation. Use with caution and avoid prolonged use without medical
supervision.
Refer to a specialist if:
The diagnosis is uncertain;
There is no improvement with standard treatment;
There are signs of severe disease (e.g., joint pain with psoriasis, severe prurigo).
Note: A detailed list of treatment options is provided in ANNEXURE 4.
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Other common and important disorders
content:
Other common and important disorders

Figure 3.6.1. Melasma
Bilateral brown pigmented patches on the face, especially on the cheeks, nose bridge
and forehead
Seen more in women than in men
Sun exposure, pregnancy, oral contraceptive pills and other risk factors trigger onset and
progression
Figure 3.6.2. Vitiligo
Loss of pigment-producing cells or melanocytes from the skin that determines the
different tones of skin and hair colour
Affects skin anywhere in the body
Occurs at any age, progressive
Affects 0.5%–2% of the population
Figure 3.6.3. Basal cell carcinoma
A common type of skin cancer originating from keratinocytes (skin cells)
Typically appears as a slowly growing plaque or nodule
May gradually enlarge to form a mass that bleeds easily
Usually localized and rarely spreads (non-invasive)
Commonly occurs on sun-exposed areas of the body
If suspected, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation and management
Figure 3.6.4. (left) and 3.6.5. (right) Squamous cell carcinoma
A common type of skin cancer originating from squamous cells (skin cells)
Typically presents as a slowly growing plaque or nodule
May enlarge to form a mass that bleeds or ulcerates easily
Unlike basal cell carcinoma, it can be invasive and may spread to other parts of the body
(metastasize)
Risk factors include chronic ulcers (from injury, burns, or disease), sun exposure,
smoking, and aging
If suspected, refer the patient to a specialist for further evaluation and management
Figure 3.6.6. Melanoma
Most serious type of skin cancer
Skin cancer of pigment-producing cells
Affects skin anywhere in the body
Warning signs: asymmetric, uneven border, various shades of black, changes in
size/shape/colour/appearance
If suspected, refer immediately to a specialist
Figure 3.6.7. (left) and 3.6.8. (right) Severe drug eruption (Stevens–Johnson
syndrome/Toxic epidermal necrolysis)
Serious reaction caused by medication
Usually develops during the first 1–2 weeks after starting the causative medication
Often begins with a painful rash
Blistering and peeling of the skin and mucous membranes (mouth, nose, eyes, genitals)
as it progresses
Flu-like symptoms (fever, sore mouth/throat, etc.) may appear before skin/mucous
membrane involvement
If suspected, refer immediately to a specialist
Stopping the causative medication is the most important

source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Use of medicated creams and ointments
content:
Use of medicated creams and ointments

Topical medications are effective in treating many of the skin diseases. It is important to remind
patients to wash their hands before and after applying the creams. Typically, it is recommended
that a thin layer of the ointment be applied and the cream massaged to the affected areas.
Regarding the amount of medication to use, one can opt for the "fingertip unit", which is the
amount of ointment or cream needed to reach from the fingertip to the first crease of the finger.
This is approximately equal to 0.5 grams. Thus, you can use the image below to estimate how
many "fingertip units" are recommended for each body part.
Figure 3.7.1. Steps for applying topical treatment
Wash hands: Start by washing your hands thoroughly with soap and water to ensure
they're clean before touching the affected area.
Apply treatment: Apply a thin layer of the treatment to the affected area. Avoid using
too much cream, as a thin layer is usually sufficient. The amount to be applied can be
estimated using the 'finger-tip-unit'.
Massage gently: Gently massage the treatment into the skin using circular motions.
Wash hands: After applying the treatment, wash your hands again to remove any
residue and prevent accidental transfer to other areas.
Fingertip unit guide:
Fingertip unit: 1
Per arm: 3
Front: 7
Back and buttocks: 7
Per hand: 1
Per leg: 6
Per foot: 2
Remember that different medicated creams may have unique application
instructions, so always read and follow the guidance provided on the product
packaging and any advice given by your healthcare professional.
For scabies treatment, do not wash the hands after applying the ointment or
cream, as the hands are one of the most commonly affected areas and need
adequate exposure to the medication.
It is important to note that each medication may have different instructions for use. Therefore,
reading the medication's specific guidance prior to use is recommended.
Caution should also be exercised regarding the overuse of certain medications, especially
topical corticosteroids. Topical steroids are typically used for eczema, psoriasis, and other
inflammatory skin diseases. Self-administration of topical steroids can be dangerous and should
not be used without medical advice. While steroids can be helpful in reducing itchiness and
inflammation, long-term use has various side-effects, including delayed wound healing, thin skin
that bruises easily and infections.
Side-effects of topical steroids Prolonged or inappropriate use of topical steroids may cause
the following side effects:
Skin-related effects: thinning of the skin, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation or
hyperpigmentation, stretch marks (especially in armpits or groin), easy bruising or
tearing of the skin, increased hair growth or thickness, redness
Hormonal effects: round face ("moon face") as seen in Cushing syndrome
Other effects: worsening of skin infections, risk of bone weakening and fractures
In children: slow growth with long-term use
subtopic: Chapter 3: Important common skin diseases in communities of the South-East Asia
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: When making a referral
content:
When making a referral

If you are unsure of the diagnosis, consider referring the patient. When immediate referral is not
possible, take clear photos of the skin lesion(s) for later review. Photos are valuable tools that
support accurate diagnosis of skin conditions. Referral should also be considered when you
suspect a serious disease or when further examination is necessary to confirm the diagnosis.
To ensure an effective referral, especially when done remotely (e.g. via telemedicine), it is
important to provide more than just a photo. Use the same approach described in this booklet
for describing skin lesions. Whenever possible, include the following information in your referral
notes:
Onset: When did the symptoms start? Was the onset sudden (acute), gradual
(subacute), or prolonged (chronic)?
Skin lesions: What types of lesions are present (e.g. papules, ulcers, patches)? Are
multiple types present?
Texture: Is the lesion soft, firm, scaly, crusted, dry, or moist?
Distribution: Where are the lesions located? Are they on one or both sides? Localized
or widespread? Symmetrical or asymmetrical?
Sensation: Is the lesion itchy, painful, or numb? Is there any loss of sensation?
You may also include additional observations such as warmth, discharge, or smell, as well as
symptoms beyond the skin, such as fever, joint pain, or swelling, that may help guide diagnosis
and treatment.
Wounds are common, especially in remote communities. They may result from a variety of
causes, such as injury, burns, infections, or underlying medical conditions, but regardless of the
cause, the basic principles of wound care remain the same. Proper wound care is essential to
prevent infection, support healing, and reduce the risk of long-term complications such as
scarring or disability.
This chapter begins with the fundamentals of wound care, followed by guidance on assessing
the cause of wounds and additional tips to promote healing. Wound care techniques can be
taught to patients and their families, so that care can continue where they live.
You can also refer to ANNEXURE 5 where it provides a flow chart to help guide wound care.
subtopic: Chapter 4: Managing wounds
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Basics of wound care
content:
Basics of wound care

There are five main principles to support and accelerate the wound healing process.
1.​ Wash the wound
2.​ Keep the wound moist
3.​ Timely dressing change
4.​ Remove dead skin, tissues and any foreign objects
5.​ Diagnose and treat infection early
1. Wash the wound
Keep the wound and surrounding skin clean by washing with clean water or a saline solution.
Wash gently. This is to wash away any bacteria or debris from the surface of the wound. Avoid
using hydrogen peroxide, alcohol or iodine products. These products may damage the newly
growing cells to heal the wound. It is also important to wear gloves, but if they are not available,
wash your hands very well with soap and water before and after touching the wound.
If you are worried that the water may not be clean, boil the water. Cool it down before using it on
the wound. Clean water means that it should be fit for drinking.
2. Keep the wound moist
The wound should not be too dry or too moist. As it is also composed of living cells such as
those in any other parts of our body, it needs some moisture for the new skin tissue to grow and
close the wound. A moist wound environment is not only good for wound healing, but it also
helps in relieving pain.
If the wound surface is dry, an ointment can be applied. Petroleum jelly is one of the best and
inexpensive ointments to apply on a wound. However, it may not always be available. Other
products or natural sources (honey, turmeric, aloe vera, etc.) can be used in community settings
as alternatives. If you are unsure about what you have is appropriate for application on a
wound, consult a specialist.
3. Timely dressing change
Wound dressings help maintain a moist environment at the wound surface, which supports
healing. Use clean gauze or cloth to cover the wound. The frequency of dressing changes
depends on the wound condition and the type of dressing used. In general, dressings should be
changed once a day or whenever they become wet or dirty.
If the wound produces excessive exudate – moisture that leaks onto the surrounding skin and
causes maceration – the dressing should be changed more frequently. For clean wounds that
are healing well, less frequent dressing changes (such as a few times per week) may be
sufficient.
Maceration
For effective wound healing, the skin around the wound (called the periwound area)
must remain healthy. Excessive exudate (fluid) from the wound can damage this
surrounding skin. Maceration happens when too much exudate makes the nearby
skin look whitish, soft, or soggy. This is a sign that the dressing may need to be
changed more often to protect the skin and support proper healing.
4. Remove dead skin and tissues and any foreign objects
Dead skin and tissues must be removed to support healing – this process is called
"debridement". Debridement can be done surgically in a sterile way with sterile sharp
instruments or, if available, chemically with ointments which help dissolve dead tissues. If bone
is exposed or can be felt, this is a strong indication of possible osteomyelitis (bone infection)
and the patient should be referred to a specialist for further evaluation and possible removal.
Any foreign objects, such as nails, small stones, or wood splinters, can also interfere with
wound healing and must be removed. People affected by leprosy or diabetes, who often have
reduced sensation, may not feel pain and therefore may not notice these objects.
Do not debride dry and intact black eschars with no evidence of infection.
5. Diagnose and treat infection early
Infection can delay wound healing. Not only it may make wound healing stagnant, it may even
worsen the wound, leading to a longer time to heal. It is therefore important to diagnose and
treat infection as early as possible.
A wound may be infected if:
it becomes red, swollen, hot, and painful;
it has pus; or
it starts to smell bad.
The infection may be spreading to other parts of the body if:
the patient has a fever;
there is lymphangitis (inflammation of the lymphatic channels); or
lymph nodes (felt as lumps in the neck, armpits, or groin) become swollen and tender.
In such cases, treat the patient with systemic antibiotics. Wash the wound thoroughly with clean
water and increase the frequency of dressing changes.
When a patient is experiencing fever and chills, suspect sepsis, which is a serious condition
that the body is over reacting and causing extreme response to the infection. The patient may
also present with altered mental status or low blood pressure (hypotension). Refer the patient
immediately to a doctor.
subtopic: Chapter 4: Managing wounds
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Assess and correct cause(s) of wound
content:
Assess and correct cause(s) of wound

Assessing and treating the underlying disease or condition are crucial for providing patients
with the right care. Wounds can occur due to various causes, ranging from trauma and burns
(external causes) to infectious to non-infectious ones (internal causes).
If it is an internal cause, treatment and management of the cause are as important as wound
care to achieve complete healing. If these causes are not managed well, it can lead to delayed
wound healing. For example, if you do not manage the blood sugar level in a patient with
diabetic foot ulcer, the wound will likely lead to a long healing course. If you see a patient with a
wound from skin tuberculosis, you need to treat for tuberculosis, only then the wound will heal.
Certain external factors can delay wound healing. For example, pressure ulcers require relief of
pressure at the wound site through frequent position changes. This is especially important for
people with diabetes or leprosy, who often have reduced sensation in their limbs.
Without normal sensation, pressure may be unevenly distributed, particularly on the soles of the
feet, resulting in wounds. In such cases, off-loading devices such as specially designed shoes
or supports are needed to reduce pressure on specific areas and allow the wound to heal.
Additionally, underlying systemic illnesses, such as anaemia, diabetes, peripheral arterial
disease (PAD), hypothyroidism (a type of autoimmune disease) and HIV/AIDS, as well as some
therapies, such as use of corticosteroids, can lead to wound healing delay. A range of daily
activities, from smoking to eating habits, can also cause wound healing delay. Understanding
the presence of these underlying conditions and correcting them are also important.
If you suspect any underlying condition from internal causes or are unsure about the cause of
the wound, refer the patient to a specialist.
subtopic: Chapter 4: Managing wounds
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Additional tips to help wound healing
content:
Additional tips to help wound healing

Manage swelling... Swelling (oedema) can slow down wound healing. For wounds on the lower
limbs, encourage patients to elevate the affected limb to reduce swelling. Compression
bandaging and gentle massage may also support the reduction of oedema and promote faster
healing.
Prevent or treat physical sequelae/disability... Wound care should aim not only for wound
closure, but also for the preservation of physical function. Patients should not be discouraged
from moving the body part affected by a wound. Instead, encourage early and safe movement
from the beginning of treatment. Prolonged immobility can lead to muscle wasting and loss of
strength, making it harder for patients to regain movement even after the wound has healed.
Advise and provide appropriate mobility aids such as crutches, walkers, or adaptive equipment,
and teach both patients and caregivers how to use them safely. Tailor these strategies to the
available resources and cultural context of the community.
Incorporating these approaches during wound care is vital to preventing physical disabilities and
helping patients maintain independence and quality of life.
Eating healthy... Good nutrition is essential for wound healing. Ensure the patient is eating a
balanced diet with adequate protein, fruits, and vegetables to support tissue repair and recovery.
Continue care after wound closure... Even after the wound has healed, care must continue. A
scarred area remains vulnerable to breakdown or recurrence of a wound. To keep the skin
healthy, apply petroleum jelly or moisturizing cream regularly to keep the skin soft and hydrated.
Also avoid putting pressure on the scar area whenever possible.
When to consider referral... If the size of a wound does not show improvement within 4–6
weeks, this indicates that additional care may be needed, and referral to a specialized facility is
recommended. Always refer the patient if the wound worsens at any point. To make informed
decisions, it is important to monitor the wound's progress by regularly taking photographs or
measuring its size and depth.
In conclusion, effective wound care requires a holistic approach. Healing depends not only on
direct wound management but also on the patient's overall health, daily practices, and living
conditions. Engaging the patient and their family in the care process is essential to ensure
adherence to treatment and to improve long-term outcomes.
Healthy skin is everyone's right – free from diseased skin. While some skin conditions, such
as atopic dermatitis, are unavoidable due to genetic predisposition, others, like injuries or
infections, may result from environmental factors such as climate, overcrowding, or poor living
conditions. These challenges are often difficult to overcome quickly.
However, many skin diseases can be prevented or better controlled through community-level
actions. Education and awareness play a crucial role. Because skin diseases are often visible,
people affected may face stigma and discrimination, which can harm both their physical and
mental health. With the right knowledge and support, communities can challenge
misconceptions and promote inclusion.
This chapter offers practical approaches for educating patients, families, and communities to
improve skin health and to support the elimination of skin-related neglected tropical diseases
(skin NTDs).
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Skin care: Key habits for healthy skin
content:
Skin care: Key habits for healthy skin

This section outlines simple, everyday practices that help maintain healthy skin and prevent
common skin conditions and infections. These key messages can be easily shared with
patients, families, and communities.
1. Daily self-care practices
These are the most important day-to-day actions that everyone can take:
Wash hands regularly – especially before eating and after using the toilet.
Bathe daily with soap.
Moisturize after bathing to prevent dry skin.
Trim fingernails regularly.
Why it matters: Clean and well-cared-for skin is essential to prevent infections, not
only of the skin, but also of the gut, eyes, lungs, and other parts of the body.
2. Keeping clothes, bedding, and surroundings clean
Regular washing of personal items and bedding is important for skin health and
infection/infestation prevention:
Clothing: Wash any soiled clothing prior to wearing. Avoid strong soaps and detergents
that may irritate the skin.
Bedding: Wash sheets and blankets at least once every week, or every two weeks. If
available, use a vacuum cleaner to remove dirt from your bedding. Hang or spread
sheets and blankets under direct sun regularly. Sunlight is a natural disinfectant and
helps kill germs.
General hygiene: Keep sleeping and living areas clean and well-ventilated. Remove
accumulated dust, sweat, and body fluids that can promote bacterial or fungal growth.
Why it matters: Clean clothes, bedding, and surroundings reduce the risk of skin
infections, infestations such as scabies, and allergic reactions caused by dust and
irritants.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Protection from the sun
content:
Protection from the sun

The sun's ultraviolet (UV) rays can damage the skin over time, leading to sunburn, premature
aging, and an increased risk of skin cancers, including melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma,
and basal cell carcinoma. Protecting the skin from the sun is therefore an important part of
maintaining long-term skin health.
Simple steps to protect the skin from sun damage:
Apply sunscreen before going outdoors, especially exposed areas like the face, arms,
and legs.
Wear sun-protective clothing, such as hats or long-sleeved shirts.
Limit time in direct sunlight by avoiding outdoor activities during peak sunlight hours (10
a.m. to 4 p.m.), and seek shade whenever possible.
It is very important to share these tips with anyone who spends a significant amount of time in
the sun, including agricultural workers and fishermen.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Protection from insect bites
content:
Protection from insect bites

Preventing insect bites is an important prevention method not only for avoiding discomfort, but
also for protecting oneself from getting infected with diseases spread by insects or for reducing
the risk of allergic reactions.
Simple steps to be protected from insect bites:
Wear protective clothing: Use long-sleeved clothing and pants, especially in areas with
high mosquito activity or in regions where insect-borne diseases are prevalent.
Use insect repellents: Apply insect repellents containing DEET, picaridin or other
recommended ingredients to exposed skin. Reapply as needed, especially during the
evening when mosquitoes are most active.
Avoid attractants: Avoid using heavily scented products and brightly coloured clothing
that may attract insects.
Use bednets and screens: In areas or housings where insects are a concern, use
bednets and screens to create a protective barrier.
Exercise caution in specific environments: Keep your surroundings clean to minimize
or eliminate breeding sites of vectors, such as stagnant water, tall grass and dense
vegetation as well as domestic water containers in your house.
Seek medical attention: In cases of severe reactions to insect bites or suspected
exposure to disease-carrying insects, seek immediate medical attention.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Seeking care at an early stage
content:
Seeking care at an early stage

Encouraging patients to check their skin
"Look, ask and feel" is not only a helpful tool for a provider when assessing skin lesions, but it is
also something that patients can adopt for protecting themselves. Encourage patients to look at
their skin often for any new or rapidly changing lesions. Further, if there are any lesions or areas
that are hard to be looked at by the patients themselves (such as their back), have them ask a
trusted family member or a friend to take a closer look. Finally, encourage them to feel the lesion
for an irregular or raised texture. If it does feel irregular or raised, the patients should seek
medical care.
Keeping first-aid supplies at home
Keep first-aid supplies, such as plasters and dressings, readily available at home. This can
prevent exposing the wound to dirt and germs at the earliest to stall secondary infections.
More awareness and seeking care at an early stage
Skin lesions are so common in the community that many people neglect the conditions. They
may think these are "a part of their lives"; they do not think that this is something for which they
should seek care or which can be treated. This can lead to delays in treatment and serious
complications. There needs to be a higher level of awareness about skin infections so that
people will seek earlier care. Similarly, there is lack of awareness about the fact that many of
these conditions can be prevented by maintaining good skin hygiene and taking care of any
known wounds. Assess your community's awareness of skin hygiene and educate.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Approaches to reducing stigma and discrimination
content:
Approaches to reducing stigma and discrimination

Many skin diseases, particularly when they affect visible parts of the body, can lead to stigma
and discrimination. This is especially true for skin NTDs, such as leprosy, which have been
among the most stigmatized conditions. However, many other skin diseases face similar
challenges.
Stigma and discrimination, often rooted within the community, are driven by misconceptions,
fear of contagion and social prejudices. In some cases, stigma may lead to isolation, affecting
not only patients but also their families. Self-stigma, wherein an individual internalizes the
negative attitudes of others, can be especially harmful, as it impacts the patient's mental
well-being and reduces his/her willingness to seek care.
You play a pivotal role in combating stigma as a health-care provider. It is important that you
treat patients with skin NTDs and other skin conditions with dignity and respect, ensuring that
your own attitudes do not contribute to the stigma. By demonstrating empathy and
professionalism, you can set an example for others in the community.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Empowering patients to take action
content:
Empowering patients to take action

As providers, it is essential to encourage patients to take action and care for themselves, as
self-care is a big part of good skin health.
Share these five key goals with your patients and answer any questions that they may have with
regard to achieving these goals:
1.​ Prove to others that you are able to take care of your skin: Ensure that patients have
a solid understanding of good skin hygiene.
2.​ Prove to others that you are able to prevent disability: It is important that patients
know and use preventive techniques (such as wearing protective shoes, applying
sunscreen and performing wound care), and prioritize including these steps in their daily
lives to maintain good skin health.
3.​ Prove that you can make your life a good example for others to follow: By adopting
these practices, patients can become a steward and encourage others to also follow
these steps.
4.​ Find ways to help other people: Completing skin checks, encouraging good skin
hygiene practices and helping others to treat their wounds can be some of the ways in
which patients can help their community members. With this united effort, patients can
support one another and the efforts of promoting skin health grow stronger. Additionally,
patients can also become community advocates for promoting policy changes and
expansion of public health efforts.
5.​ At all times, remember that you are special: Living with a skin disease can take a
great mental toll, especially for diseases that carry stigma in the community.
Encouraging love for self is fundamental to the success of skin disease treatment.
Conclusion
This booklet adopts a skin sign and symptom-based approach to skin NTDs and other skin
diseases, moving beyond the traditional disease-specific focus, often found in previous training
materials. By emphasizing the recognition of the syndromes and patterns instead of just
individual diseases, this approach is designed to better align with your day-to-day clinical
practice, helping you to identify and manage a broad range of skin conditions.
For any disease control efforts to be successful, community engagement is vital. Because most
skin diseases do not cause immediate death, they are often overlooked by communities.
Sensitization to improving the skin health of the community is crucial. As a front-line health-care
worker, you are at the forefront of this effort to bring about a positive change. Your role goes
beyond diagnosing and treating patients with skin diseases – you have a unique opportunity
to motivate, educate and engage your community in preventing skin diseases and
promoting early access to care.
If the health-seeking behaviour is such that an individual accesses health-care facilities when
he/she first notices his/her abnormal skin condition, there will be fewer delays in diagnosis and
treatment of skin NTDs and other debilitating skin diseases. The skin, too frequently
overlooked, is an important indicator of overall health and maintaining healthy skin
contributes to the well-being of the entire community.
As you continue your essential work, this booklet is intended to be a practical resource to
support you in improving skin health in your communities. We hope it equips you with the
knowledge and confidence needed to manage skin NTDs and other skin diseases effectively,
thereby helping reduce the burden of skin diseases in the regions where you serve.
subtopic: Chapter 5: Educating and counselling patients, families and communities
source: Integrated Approach to Management of Skin-Related Neglected Tropical Diseases and Common Skin Conditions (WHO, CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO)

title: Roller bandage
content:
Roller bandage
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: A roller bandage holds a dressing in place over a wound. It is usually made of gauze or gauze-like material and comes in widths from ½ to 12 inches. The manual suggests a narrow roll for a hand or wrist, a medium-width roll for an arm or ankle, and a wide roll for a leg.
How to use:
1. Place the dressing over the wound and secure the end of the roller bandage with one turn.
2. Wrap in overlapping turns until the dressing is completely covered.
3. Tie or tape the bandage in place.
4. Check the fingers or toes for feeling, warmth, and color. If they become cold, numb, or discolored, loosen the wrap and check again.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Adhesive bandage for a small cut or scrape
content:
Adhesive bandage for a small cut or scrape
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: An adhesive bandage has a small nonstick pad attached to an adhesive backing. It covers a minor wound that fits entirely under the pad.
How to use:
1. If the wound is bleeding, apply direct pressure with a sterile gauze.
2. Once the bleeding stops, clean the wound with soap and water.
3. Center the pad over the wound and press the adhesive edges onto the surrounding skin.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Sterile gauze pad or nonstick dressing for a larger scrape or minor open wound
content:
Sterile gauze pad or nonstick dressing for a larger scrape or minor open wound
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: A sterile pad covers a wound that needs more coverage than a small adhesive bandage provides. Gauze absorbs blood, and a nonstick dressing helps keep the pad from sticking to the wound.
How to use:
1. If there is minor bleeding, apply direct pressure with sterile gauze until it stops.
2. Clean the wound. The manual suggests rinsing a scrape under clean running water for about five minutes when possible.
3. Place a sterile pad large enough to cover the entire wound.
4. Secure the pad with a bandage.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Bandage compress for a bleeding wound
content:
Bandage compress for a bleeding wound
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: A bandage compress combines a thick gauze pad with an attached bandage. The pad absorbs blood, and the wrap holds it in place.
How to use:
1. Place the gauze pad directly over the wound and apply firm, steady pressure.
2. If bleeding is heavy or continuous, call emergency services and keep applying direct pressure.
3. Once the bleeding is controlled, secure the dressing and check circulation beyond the injury. Current Red Cross guidance says to leave the original pad in place during direct pressure and avoid stacking multiple pads.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Elastic roller bandage for a sprain or swollen joint
content:
Elastic roller bandage for a sprain or swollen joint
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: An elastic wrap can support an injured limb or joint and help control swelling.
How to use:
1. Before wrapping, check the fingers or toes for feeling, warmth, and color.
2. Wrap with overlapping turns and gently stretch the bandage as you go. The manual describes using figure-eight turns around a knee or ankle for support.
3. Check that a finger can slide under the wrap without the bandage feeling loose.
4. Check feeling, warmth, and color again after wrapping.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Sterile dressing for a heat burn
content:
Sterile dressing for a heat burn
Source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual
What it is used for: A sterile dressing protects burned skin after cooling. The manual includes this covering step for thermal burns and advises leaving burn blisters intact.
How to use:
1. Cool the burn with clean running water.
2. Cover the area loosely with a sterile dressing.
3. Leave any blisters intact.

source: First Aid/CPR/AED Participant's Manual

title: Sterile gauze pad or compress
content:
Sterile gauze pad or compress
Source: First Aid Pocket Guide
What it is used for: A sterile dressing covers an open wound, absorbs blood and other fluids, and helps protect it from contamination. The guide lists roller gauze and square pads as examples.
How to use:
1. Handle the dressing carefully. Keep the side that will touch the wound clean.
2. Place the dressing directly over the wound and make sure it covers the entire area.
3. If you need to hold the dressing in place, secure it with a clean bandage.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid Pocket Guide

title: Triangular bandage or cravat
content:
Triangular bandage or cravat
Source: First Aid Pocket Guide
What it is used for: A triangular bandage is a piece of cloth that can support an arm as a sling. A cravat is a triangular bandage folded into a broad or narrow strip. The guide lists securing a splint as another use of bandages.
How to use:
1. Use the cloth in its triangular shape for a sling or fold it into a strip for a cravat.
2. When tying the ends, use a square knot. Cross right over left, then left over right.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: First Aid Pocket Guide

title: Sterile gauze pad and bandage for an open wound
content:
Sterile gauze pad and bandage for an open wound
Source: Philippine Red Cross First Aid Support
What it is used for: A sterile dressing covers the wound, absorbs blood or other fluid, and helps protect the area from contamination. The module identifies abrasions (scrapes), lacerations (cuts or tears), punctures, and avulsions as types of open wounds.
How to use:
1. Control the bleeding.
2. Cover the wound with a sterile dressing, such as a sterile gauze pad.
3. Secure the dressing with a bandage.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages
source: Philippine Red Cross First Aid Support

title: Clean cloth as an improvised dressing
content:
Clean cloth as an improvised dressing
Source: St. John Ambulance First Aid Reference Guide
What it is used for: A clean cloth can cover a wound when a prepared dressing is unavailable. The guide lists cotton clothing and towels as examples and recommends choosing material that is clean, preferably sterile, absorbent, lint-free, and unlikely to stick.
How to use:
1. Choose a clean piece large enough to extend beyond the wound edges.
2. Keep the surface that will touch the wound clean.
3. Place it over the wound and secure it with tape or a bandage.
subtopic: Dressings and bandages

title: BIOGESIC (Paracetamol)
content:
BIOGESIC
Manufacturer: UNILAB, Inc — Non-Rx
Composition: Paracetamol
Indications: Relief of minor aches & pains eg, headache, backache, menstrual cramps, muscular aches, minor arthritis pain, toothache & pain associated w/ common cold & flu.
Dosage: Adult & childn >12 yr 1-2 tab 4-6 hrly as needed. Max: 8 tab in 24 hr.
Administration: Take with or without food.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Anemia, cardiac & pulmonary disease. Hepatic or severe renal disease.
Special Precautions: Liver warning & disease. Other medicines containing paracetamol. Concomitant use of warfarin.
Adverse Reactions: Allergic skin reactions, GI disturbances & changes in the number of WBC & platelets.
Interactions: Anticonvulsants, aspirin, INH, phenothiazines, alcohol.
Presentation & Packing: Tab 500 mg x 20's, 500's.
subtopic: Analgesics & Antipyretics

title: BENADRYL ONE (Cetirizine HCl)
content:
BENADRYL ONE
Manufacturer: Interphil [JNTL Consumer Health] — Non-Rx
Composition: Cetirizine HCl
Indications: Symptomatic relief of allergic conditions including rhinitis & chronic urticaria.
Dosage: Adult & childn ≥6 yr 10 mg daily. Seasonal rhinitis Give at beginning of hay fever season when pollens are still few. Hepatic & renal impairment Reduce dose to ½ of usual daily dose.
Administration: Take with or without food.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to cetirizine or hydroxyzine. Not recommended to hypokalemic patients w/ chronic renal failure undergoing hemodialysis. Not to be given to childn <6 yr w/ hepatic & renal impairment.
Special Precautions: Caution in patients who require mental alertness or physical coordination (eg, drivers or machine operators) since this may cause drowsiness. Pregnancy. Not recommended in lactating mothers. Not to be given to childn & infants. Elderly w/ most likely renal & hepatic impairment.
Adverse Reactions: Drowsiness; irritability, insomnia, somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, pharyngitis, dizziness, headache, abdominal pain, cough, diarrhea, epistaxis, bronchospasm, nausea & vomiting & hypersensitivity manifested by urticarial & fixed drug eruptions.
Interactions: Sedation may be enhanced w/ CNS depressants eg, barbiturates, alcohol, hypnotics, opioid analgesics, anxiolytic sedatives & neuroleptics. Enhanced effects of alcohol & other CNS depressants.
Presentation & Packing: FC tab 10 mg x 4's, 100's.
subtopic: Antihistamines & Antiallergics
source: MIMS (Monthly Index of Medical Specialties)

title: ALLERMED (Cetirizine diHCl)
content:
ALLERMED
Manufacturer: Nutramedica — FC tab/Oral soln: Rx; Oral drops: Non-Rx
Composition: Cetirizine diHCl
Indications: Perennial rhinitis, seasonal allergic rhinitis, chronic idiopathic urticaria & allergic conjunctivitis.
Dosage: Tab Adult & childn ≥6 yr 10 mg/day or 5 mg bid. Childn 2-5 yr 5 mg/day as single dose or 2.5 mg bid every after 12 hr, 6 mth-2 yr Initially 2.5 mg/day. Max: 5 mg/day given bid. Hepatic & renal impairment Reduce dose to ½ the usual dose per day. Oral soln Adult & childn >12 yr 10 mL daily. Childn 6-12 yr 10 mL daily as single dose or 5 mL bid preferably morning & evening, 2-5 yr 2.5 mL bid. Oral drops Adult & childn >12 yr 20 drops once daily. Childn 6-12 yr 20 drops once daily or 10 drops bid (as divided doses in the morning & evening); 2-5 yr 10 drops once daily or 5 drops bid (as divided doses in the morning & evening); 6 mth-2 yr 5 drops once daily or 2.5 drops bid (as divided doses in the morning & evening).
Administration: Take with or without food.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to antihistamines. History of unusual severe reactions eg, excessive sedation or CNS stimulation. Prostatic hypertrophy, narrow-angle glaucoma. Neonates & preterm/premature infants.
Special Precautions: Patients w/ renal impairment; epilepsy, severe CV disorders. Avoid alcoholic drink. May affect ability to drive or operate machinery. Pregnancy. Infants (premature) & neonates. Elderly.
Adverse Reactions: Drowsiness; irritability, insomnia, somnolence, fatigue, dry mouth, pharyngitis, dizziness, headache, abdominal pain, cough, diarrhea, epistaxis, bronchospasm, nausea, vomiting, urticaria, fixed drug eruptions. Oral drops: Hypotension, tinnitus, paresthesias, GI disturbances & blood disorders.
Interactions: May enhance sedative effects of CNS depressants eg, alcohol, barbiturates, hypnotics, opioid analgesics, anxiolytic sedatives, neuroleptics. Enhanced antimuscarinic effects w/ MAOIs. Additive antimuscarinic action w/ atropine, TCAs. Higher incidence of adverse effects especially CNS stimulation & insomnia w/ oral decongestants.
Presentation & Packing: FC tab 10 mg x 100's. Oral soln 1 mg/mL x 30 mL, 60 mL. Oral drops 2.5 mg/mL x 15 mL.
subtopic: Antihistamines & Antiallergics
source: MIMS (Monthly Index of Medical Specialties)

title: ADVIL (Ibuprofen)
content:
ADVIL
Manufacturer: Catalent Pharma [Haleon] — Non-Rx
Composition: Ibuprofen
Indications: Reduction of fever. Relief of mild to moderate pain & inflammation associated w/ dysmenorrhea, headache including migraine, post-op & dental pain, musculoskeletal & joint disorders eg, ankylosing spondylitis, OA & RA including juvenile idiopathic arthritis. Periarticular disorders eg, bursitis & tenosynovitis & soft tissue disorders eg, sprains & strains.
Dosage: Adult 1-2 softgel cap every 4-6 hr. Max: 6 softgel caps.
Administration: Take immediately after meals.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity. Concurrent or previous history of GI bleeding or ulceration. Pregnancy (last trimester).
Special Precautions: Asthma, heart disease, liver cirrhosis, HTN, kidney disease or taking other NSAIDs. Discontinue if severe allergic reaction including skin reddening, rash & blisters occur. Increase risk of heart attack or stroke in long-term use. Pregnancy & lactation. Elderly. Childn <12 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea w/ or w/o vomiting, GI bleeding & ulceration; broad range of hematologic, cardiac, GI, hepatic, renal, CNS, resp & dermatologic reactions as detailed in the source.
Interactions: NSAIDs, anticoagulants. Increased risk of GI bleeding w/ SSRIs. Increased plasma conc of lithium.
Presentation & Packing: Softgel 200 mg x 10's, 100's.
subtopic: Analgesics, Antipyretics & Anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs)
source: MIMS (Monthly Index of Medical Specialties)

title: ADVIL SUSPENSION FOR KIDS (Ibuprofen)
content:
ADVIL SUSPENSION FOR KIDS
Manufacturer: Interphil [Haleon] — Non-Rx
Composition: Ibuprofen
Indications: Fever & pains due to headache & toothache, & those associated w/ colds, flu & sore throat.
Dosage: Childn 11-12 yr or 33-43 kg 15 mL every 6 hr. Max: 1,200 mg. 9-10 yr or 27-32 kg 12.5 mL every 6 hr. Max: 1,000 mg. 6-8 yr or 22-26 kg 10 mL every 6 hr. Max: 800 mg. 4-5 yr or 16-21 kg 7.5 mL every 6 hr. Max: 600 mg. 2-3 yr or 11-15 kg 5 mL every 6 hr. Max: 400 mg.
Administration: Take immediately after meals.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ibuprofen, aspirin, NSAIDs. Concurrent or previous history of GI bleeding or ulceration.
Special Precautions: Do not give in patients w/ asthma, heart or kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, HTN, developed allergic reaction. Increased risk of heart attack or stroke (long-term continuous use). Inadequate fluid intake or lost fluids due to continuous vomiting or diarrhea in childn <12 yr. Discontinue use if pain gets worse or lasts >10 days & if fever persists or lasts >3 days; red or swollen painful area or blood in vomit or bloody stool appear. Childn <2 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea w/ or w/o vomiting, GI bleeding & ulceration; broad range of hematologic, cardiac, GI, hepatic, renal, CNS, resp & dermatologic reactions (including SJS, TEN, erythema multiforme) as detailed in the source.
Interactions: Other NSAIDs, anticoagulants. Increased risk of GI bleeding w/ SSRIs. Increased plasma conc of lithium.
Presentation & Packing: Oral susp 100 mg/5 mL x 60 mL.

title: PONSER (Mefenamic acid)
content:
PONSER
Manufacturer: Medhaus — 250-mg cap: Non-Rx; 500-mg cap/susp: Rx
Composition: Mefenamic acid
Indications: Relief of mild to moderately severe somatic & neuritic pain eg, headache, migraine, traumatic pain, postpartum, post-op & dental pain; pain conditions: dysmenorrheal, hemorralgia, accompanied by spasm or hypogastric pain.
Dosage: 500 mg tab 1 tab tid. Cap 1-2 cap tid. Oral susp Childn 9-12 yr 20 mL, 5-<9 yr 15 mL, 2-5 yr 10 mL, 6 mth-<2 yr 5 mL. Repeated up to tid as necessary. Should not be given >7 days.
Administration: Take immediately after meals.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity to aspirin or any other NSAIDs. Inflammatory bowel disease, peptic & intestinal ulceration. CVA, MI, coronary artery bypass graft, uncontrolled HTN, CHF NYHA II-IV. Previous or active peptic ulceration. Cardiac disease. Renal & hepatic impairment.
Special Precautions: Dehydration & renal disease. Pregnancy. Elderly. Childn <14 yr.
Adverse Reactions: GI discomfort, diarrhea or gas constipation, nausea, vomiting, drowsiness & dizziness.
Interactions: Plasma protein binding drugs. Anticoagulants.
Presentation & Packing: Tab 500 mg x 100's. Cap 500 mg x 100's, 250 mg x 100's. Oral susp 50 mg/5 mL x 60 mL.

title: RITEMED MEFENAMIC ACID (Mefenamic acid)
content:
RITEMED MEFENAMIC ACID
Manufacturer: RiteMED [United Lab] — 250 mg: Non-Rx; 500 mg: Rx
Composition: Mefenamic acid
Indications: Relief of mild to moderate pain eg, headache, dental pain, pain after childbirth or surgery, primary dysmenorrhea, & menorrhagia (heavy menstrual period) due to dysfunctional causes. Relief of pain associated w/ musculoskeletal & joint disorders including OA & RA.
Dosage: Adult & childn >14 yr 1-2 tabs 250 mg tab or 1 tab 500 mg every 8 hr. Relief of dysmenorrhea & premenstrual syndrome 1-2 tabs 250 mg tab or 1 tab 500 mg every 8 hr, should not be given for >7 days.
Administration: Take immediately after meals.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity w/ mefenamic acid, aspirin or any other NSAID. Patient currently taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Patient had or is suffering from stomach ulcers, bleeding or other stomach problems eg, inflammatory bowel disease; diarrhea w/ mefenamic acid in the past. Severe heart, liver or kidney disease, bleeding in the brain or other bleeding disorders, high K in the blood, dengue fever. Pre-op pain in the setting of CABG surgery. Pregnancy (3rd trimester). Lactation. Childn & adolescent <14 yr. 250 mg: Bronchospasm, angioedema, nasal polyps or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. 500 mg: Asthma, urticaria.
Special Precautions: May increase risk of serious CV thrombotic events, MI, & stroke; patients w/ CV disease or risk factors for CV disease; ischemic heart disease (eg, MI &/or angina), cerebrovascular disease (eg, stroke, CVA, transient ischemic attacks &/or amaurosis fugax) &/or CHF. Serious GI adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, & perforation of the stomach, small or large intestines; increased stomach bleeding risk in patients w/ stomach ulcers or bleeding problems; taking blood thinning (anticoagulant) or steroid medicine; medicines containing prescription or nonprescription NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen or others); takes 3 or more alcoholic drinks everyday; prolonged use may increase risk of heart attack or stroke. Elderly patients suffering from dehydration & kidney disease. Not recommended for use w/ other NSAIDs, w/ the exception of low-dose aspirin for CV prophylaxis. Interferes w/ platelet function; used w/ caution in patients w/ intracranial hemorrhage & bleeding diathesis. Onset of new or worsening of preexisting HTN; closely monitor BP during initiation & throughout the course of therapy. Caution in patients w/ fluid retention or heart failure. Patients on prolonged corticosteroid therapy should be tapered slowly. Administration of NSAID may cause a dose-dependent reduction in prostaglandin formation & in renal blood flow which may precipitate overt renal decompensation. Patients at greater risk of are those w/ impaired renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, taking diuretics & ACE inhibitors. Administer w/ caution to patients w/ preexisting asthma. Discontinue use at the 1st appearance of skin rash, mucosal lesions, or any sign of hypersensitivity. Check for Hb or hematocrit in patients w/ long-term treatment w/ NSAIDs. Patients w/ symptoms &/or signs suggesting liver dysfunction, or in whom an abnormal liver test occurs should be evaluated. Discontinue if clinical signs & symptoms consistent w/ liver disease develop or if systemic manifestations occur (eg, eosinophilia, rash). Prolonged use of any types of analgesic may worsen headache. Increased risk of aseptic meningitis. Caution should be exercised in patients suffering from epilepsy. Liver dysfunction, rash, blood dyscrasias or development of diarrhea should be monitored in patients on prolonged therapy. May affect the ability to drive & use machine. Not recommended in patients w/ advanced renal disease. Elderly. Childn & adolescent <14 yr.
Adverse Reactions: Abdominal pain, abnormal kidney function, anemia, constipation, diarrhea, dyspepsia, edema, dizziness, elevated liver enzymes (eg, ALT or AST), flatulence, GI ulcers (gastric/duodenal), gross bleeding/perforation, headache, heartburn, increased bleeding time, itching, nausea, rashes, ringing in the ears (tinnitus), & vomiting.
Interactions: Increase risk of renal impairment w/ ACE inhibitors (eg, captopril, fosinopril, imidapril, enalapril) & AIIA (eg, losartan, telmisartan). May reduce excretion of aminoglycosides (eg, gentamicin) & MTX. Increased Cmax & AUC w/ antacid. Increased risk of ulceration or bleeding w/ anticoagulants (eg, warfarin), antiplatelet agents (eg, aspirin), corticosteroids & SSRIs (eg, fluoxetine, citalopram, sertraline). Increased adverse effects w/ aspirin, other NSAIDs (eg, ibuprofen, ketorolac, meloxicam) including COX-2 selective inhibitors (eg, celecoxib, etoricoxib). Reduced GFR & increase plasma cardiac glycoside levels w/ cardiac glycosides (eg, digoxin). Increased risk of nephrotoxicity w/ ciclosporin & tacrolimus. Reduced the natriuretic effects of diuretics (eg, thiazides, furosemide). Altered safety & efficacy w/ drugs affecting hepatic microsomal enzymes. Reduce renal excretion w/ lithium. Concomitant use w/ mifepristone can reduce its effects. Increased risk of hypoglycemia. Reduced metabolism & prolonged t½ w/ oral hypoglycemic agents (sulfonylureas eg, gliclazide, glipizide, glimepiride). Reduced metabolism & elimination w/ probenecid. Concomitant use w/ protein-bound drugs (eg, hydantoins, sulfonamides & sulfonylureas). Increased risk of convulsions w/ quinolones antibiotics. Increased risk of hematological toxicity w/ zidovudine.
Presentation & Packing: Tab 250 mg x 100's. 500 mg x 100's.
subtopic: Analgesics & Anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs)

title: HANSOL (Chlorhexidine gluconate)
content:
HANSOL
Manufacturer: Sirmaxo Chemicals [Detoxicare] — Non-Rx
Composition: Chlorhexidine gluconate
Indications: Pre-op surgical hand disinfection, antiseptic hand washing on the ward & pre-op & post-op skin antisepsis for patients undergoing elective surgery.
Dosage: Use undiluted. Adult - hand washing: put 5 mL onto wet hands; wash for 30 sec then rinse thoroughly & dry. Surgical hand washing: put 5 mL onto wet hands & wash for 2 min; rinse thoroughly & dry w/ sterile towel. Body cleansing: lather sufficient amount on wet body; wash as usual then rinse thoroughly & dry. Childn & elderly: use normal adult dose.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity.
Special Precautions: For external use only. Do not inj or use in body cavities. Do not mix w/ detergents or other chemicals. Avoid contact w/ eyes, brain, meninges & middle ear. If come in contact w/ eyes, wash promptly & thoroughly w/ water.
Presentation & Packing: Topical soln 4% w/v x 100 mL x 1's, 500 mL x 1's.
subtopic: Antiseptics & Disinfectants
source: MIMS (Monthly Index of Medical Specialties)

title: SANISCRUB E (Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.5% w/v, ethanol 70% v/v)
content:
SANISCRUB E
Manufacturer: Sirmaxo Chemicals [Detoxicare] — Non-Rx
Composition: Chlorhexidine gluconate 0.5% w/v, ethanol 70% v/v
Indications: Rapid hand antisepsis & skin antisepsis.
Dosage: Use undiluted. Rapid hand antisepsis: dispense 3-4 mL to moisten hands & fingernails, rub vigorously over all surfaces for 30 sec. Surgical hand antisepsis: dispense 6 mL in hands & rub on hands & forearms for 1.5-3 min specially to fingertips & areas around the nails. Skin antisepsis: apply on operative & pre-op skin area to be treated, allow to dry up to 30 sec before procedure. Apply 2-3 times for optimal results.
Contraindications: Hypersensitivity.
Special Precautions: Avoid direct contact w/ eyes & ears. Keep away from naked flame, source of heat, open live electric wire.
Adverse Reactions: Irritative skin reactions. Generalized allergic reactions (extremely rare).
Interactions: Avoid storage w/ oxidizers, strong alkalis & strong acids.
Presentation & Packing: Soln 100 mL x 1's, 500 mL x 1's.
subtopic: Antiseptics & Disinfectants

title: BETADINE SKIN CLEANSER (Povidone-iodine)
content:
BETADINE SKIN CLEANSER
Manufacturer: Interphil [iNova] — Non-Rx
Composition: Povidone-iodine
Indications: For general hygiene & for cleansing & disinfecting the skin, against infections due to MRSA, flu (influenza, avian, swine), SARS-coronavirus, colds (rhinovirus, coronavirus) & ebola; helps stop spread of infections in acne, pimple, minor cuts & wounds; helps remove offensive odor of the underarms, feet & body; helps prevent spread of fungal infections eg, tinea pedis (athletes foot or alipunga), tinea versicolor (ringworm or an-an), tinea cruris (jock itch or hadhad). As a surgical scrub; helps relieve skin itching.
Dosage: Pour small amount on palm & dilute w/ a palmful of water. Work into a lather on skin eg, liqd soap for 15 sec. Rinse thoroughly w/ water. For body odor, use regularly until odor is removed.
Special Precautions: Iodine idiosyncrasy.
Adverse Reactions: Local irritation (discontinue).
Presentation & Packing: Cleanser 7.5% x 60 mL, 120 mL, 1 gal.
subtopic: Antiseptics & Disinfectants

title: BETADINE WOUND SOLUTION (Povidone-iodine)
content:
BETADINE WOUND SOLUTION
Manufacturer: Interphil [iNova] — Non-Rx
Composition: Povidone-iodine
Indications: Treatment & prevention of infection of minor wounds (cuts & abrasions), ulcers & burns. Pre-op disinfection of skin. Hygienic hand & skin disinfection & surgical hand disinfection.
Dosage: Minor wounds & ulcers: clean the wound area & apply undiluted once daily or bid until wound or ulcer has healed; if necessary, apply a dressing. Pre-op surgical disinfection: apply undiluted to the area & allow to dry. Hand disinfection: apply approx 3 mL undiluted onto the hands, rub into hands & around the fingers, & leave on for 1 min before washing off. Skin disinfection: apply adequate amount to the affected area & allow to dry. Surgical hand disinfection: apply approx 3 mL undiluted onto the hands, rub into hands & around the fingers, & leave on for 5 min before washing off.
Special Precautions: Iodine idiosyncrasy. Avoid pooling under the patient & in skin folds during pre-op surgery to avoid skin burn.
Adverse Reactions: Local irritation (discontinue).
Presentation & Packing: Topical soln 7.5 mL x 1's, 15 mL, 25 mL, 60 mL, 120 mL, 1 gal
